subject: Architecture
title: The Sampoong Department Store Collapse
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Sampoong Department Store Collapse.

hook.text: In 1995, a South Korean mall collapsed in 20 seconds, killing 502 people — the worst peacetime building disaster.

buildup.text: The owner illegally added a fifth floor and a heavy rooftop restaurant after the building was already complete.

discovery.text: Cracks appeared in the ceiling that morning. The owner refused to evacuate — he didn't want to lose sales.

twist.text: The building's columns were thinner than the original design specified. Inspectors had been bribed to approve them.

climax.text: The disaster led to South Korea's most sweeping building safety reforms — and criminal charges for the owner.

punchline.text: Greed added floors. Corruption thinned columns. Physics doesn't negotiate.

quiz.question: Why did the owner refuse to evacuate the Sampoong store?
options: He believed the cracks were only cosmetic damage
He didn't want to lose sales revenue
Engineers told him the building was still safe

details.summary: Seoul's Sampoong Department Store collapsed on June 29, 1995, killing 502 people in South Korea's deadliest peacetime disaster. The five-story building failed because its owner had overloaded the structure by adding an unauthorized floor and ignoring engineers' warnings about visible cracking.
details.whyItMatters: Sampoong is a textbook case of what happens when profit overrides safety. Ignored warnings, corrupted inspections, and unauthorized modifications converged to create a preventable tragedy that reshaped Korean building regulations.
takeaways: The Sampoong Department Store collapse killed 502 people in 1995
Unauthorized modifications and ignored warnings caused the failure
It was South Korea's deadliest peacetime disaster

faq.question: What caused the Sampoong Department Store collapse?
faq.answer: The owner added an unauthorized fifth floor and rooftop restaurant, overloading columns designed for four stories. He then moved heavy air conditioning units to the roof, exceeding structural capacity. Visible cracks were reported and ignored.

faq.question: Could it have been prevented?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Cracks were visible for months. Engineers warned the owner, who kept the store open to avoid losing revenue. The day of the collapse, an emergency inspection confirmed imminent danger, but management only closed the top floor and allowed shopping to continue below.
